what_its_for: Givosiran is used to treat adults with acute hepatic porphyria (AHP), a rare genetic condition that can cause severe attacks of belly pain, nausea, vomiting, and other serious symptoms. It works by lowering the levels of harmful substances in your body that build up and cause these attacks.
how_to_take: Givosiran is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in your belly (abdomen), upper arm, or thigh. It is given once a month by a healthcare provider, or you may be taught how to give it to yourself at home after proper training. Rotate the injection site each month and never inject into skin that is red, bruised, tender, or hard.
dosing: The usual dose is 2.5 mg per kilogram of your body weight, injected under the skin once every month. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose that is right for you based on your weight. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss your monthly dose, give the injection as soon as you remember. After that, go back to your regular monthly schedule. Do not give two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store givosiran in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do not freeze it. If needed, you may store it at room temperature (up to 86°F or 30°C) for up to 6 months, but once removed from the refrigerator, do not put it back. Keep it out of reach of children. Throw away any unused medication properly — ask your pharmacist how to dispose of it safely.
what_to_avoid: Avoid starting new medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements without telling your doctor first, because many drugs can interact with givosiran. In particular, avoid medicines that are broken down by the liver enzyme CYP1A2 (such as certain antidepressants, caffeine-containing products in large amounts, and some other drugs) unless your doctor approves. Avoid alcohol, as it may worsen liver problems. Do not inject into skin that appears irritated, scarred, or unhealthy.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: severe allergic reaction symptoms such as rash, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, dizziness, or trouble breathing; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, or right-sided stomach pain; signs of kidney problems such as decreased urination, swelling in your legs or ankles, or unusual fatigue; injection site reactions that are severe or do not go away; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Givosiran starts working within a few weeks, but you may not notice the full benefit right away. Most patients experience fewer and less severe porphyria attacks over time, often within the first few months of treatment. It is important to keep taking it every month as prescribed, even if you feel well, to prevent future attacks.
special_populations: Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor will monitor your kidney and liver function regularly during treatment, as givosiran can sometimes affect them. Dose adjustments may be needed. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of givosiran during pregnancy is not fully known, so discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Children: Givosiran is currently approved for adults only. Older adults: No special dose adjustment is needed for older adults, but close monitoring is recommended.
